notice: Harm-reduction index of documented psychoactive substances, plants and fungi people encounter, common adulterants, and medicines that change interaction risk. It is not every chemical in existence, and it is not a dose, a source, or a synthesis guide. A missing interaction is unknown risk, not a clearance.

drugs.name: Morphine
drugs.summary: Morphine is filed here as a harm-reduction record. The reference opioid. Breathing slows as the effect deepens, and hospital vials and street material are not interchangeable. This is not a dose, a source, or a reason to use it.
drugs.history: Morphine is part of the public scientific and medical record, with a commonly cited date around 1804. Legal and medical status have changed over time and still differ by country. The reference opioid. Breathing slows as the effect deepens, and hospital vials and street material are not interchangeable.
drugs.legal_status: Control status depends on the country, the form, and sometimes the amount. This file is not legal advice.
drugs.medical_status: Licensed as a medicine in at least some countries. A prescription is not a clearance to mix it or to use it outside medical care.
drugs.chemistry: Opioid. Named here so the breathing risk can be recognised. Manufacture and extraction are outside this archive.
drugs.mechanism: Mu-opioid receptor activity. Breathing slows as the effect deepens.
drugs.onset: Depends on the substance and the route. Some act in minutes. Others take much longer, which is when people get into trouble by taking more.
drugs.duration: Often several hours. Some synthetic opioids last much longer than naloxone.
drugs.half_life: Ranges from short to very long. A person can look awake and still stop breathing later.
drugs.acute_risks: The acute danger is slowed or stopped breathing. Alcohol, benzodiazepines, and other sedatives multiply that risk. Non-pharmaceutical material may contain fentanyl, nitazenes, or xylazine. The reference opioid. Breathing slows as the effect deepens, and hospital vials and street material are not interchangeable.
drugs.chronic_risks: Tolerance, dependence, constipation, low sex hormones, and fatal overdose are the main long-term harms.
drugs.overdose_signs: Slow or stopped breathing, blue or grey lips, gurgling, unresponsiveness, pinpoint pupils. This is an emergency. Naloxone can reverse the opioid and may need repeating.
drugs.dependence: Physical dependence is common with repeated use.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance rises with repeated use, then falls after a break. A familiar amount can become fatal after a pause.
drugs.withdrawal: Withdrawal feels like a severe flu with cramps, sweating, and distress. It is rarely fatal by itself and it raises the chance of returning to use.
drugs.medical_uses: Some opioids are pain or addiction medicines. Many have no accepted role outside a hospital, or none at all.
drugs.contraindications: Other sedatives, sleep apnoea, severe lung disease, and unknown-strength material.
drugs.testing: Fentanyl strips and reagent colours miss analogues and do not measure strength. A negative test is not proof of safety.
drugs.harm_reduction: Do not use alone. Keep naloxone nearby and make sure another person knows how to use it. A blank mix result is not a green light. This file has no dose.

drugs.chemistry: Cannabinoid. Plant cannabinoids and synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonists are not the same risk. Synthesis is outside this archive.
drugs.mechanism: Cannabinoid receptor activity. Synthetic cannabinoids can be full agonists and far stronger than THC.
drugs.onset: Minutes when inhaled, longer when swallowed. Swallowed THC can take hours and then last a long time.
drugs.duration: A few hours for inhaled THC. Swallowed THC and many synthetic cannabinoids last much longer.
drugs.half_life: THC leaves the blood slowly and can be detectable long after impairment fades. That is not a dosing fact.
drugs.acute_risks: Panic, vomiting, fast heart rate, and impaired driving. Synthetic cannabinoids also cause collapse, seizures, kidney injury, and death. The main intoxicating cannabinoid in cannabis. Anxiety, fast heart rate, impaired driving, and dependence are the established harms. Swallowed THC arrives late and lasts longer.
drugs.chronic_risks: Dependence, worsened anxiety, and in frequent heavy THC use a higher rate of psychotic episodes in vulnerable people. Smoking adds lung harm.
drugs.overdose_signs: For THC, severe anxiety and vomiting are the usual ceiling. For synthetic cannabinoids: collapse, seizures, chest pain, and unresponsiveness are emergencies.
drugs.dependence: Cannabis dependence is real. Withdrawal is uncomfortable rather than medically dangerous.
drugs.tolerance: The effect fades with daily use. Synthetic cannabinoids can escalate very quickly.
drugs.withdrawal: Irritability, poor sleep, low appetite, and vivid dreams for several days after stopping heavy cannabis use.
drugs.medical_uses: A few cannabinoid medicines exist. Herbal cannabis and synthetic cannabinoids sold as incense are not those medicines.
drugs.contraindications: Personal or family psychosis, pregnancy, heart disease, and any product sold as incense or 'not for human consumption'.
drugs.testing: There is no home test that makes a synthetic cannabinoid product safe. THC percentage on a label is not the batch in front of you.
drugs.harm_reduction: Do not drive. Treat any synthetic cannabinoid product as a medical emergency risk, not as cannabis. This file has no dose.

classes.description: Substances that act on opioid receptors. The acute danger is slowed or stopped breathing, especially with sedatives.

classes.name: Stimulant
classes.description: Substances that speed up the nervous system. The acute dangers are overheating, heart strain, seizures, and psychosis.

classes.name: Depressant
classes.description: Sedatives including alcohol, GHB, barbiturates, and related drugs. They slow the brain and can stop breathing.

classes.name: Benzodiazepine
classes.description: Sedating medicines and unregulated relatives. They cause blackouts and, with opioids or alcohol, stopped breathing.

classes.name: Psychedelic
classes.description: Substances that alter perception and thinking. Some are physiologically harsh. Set, setting, and other medicines matter.

classes.name: Dissociative
classes.description: NMDA-active substances such as ketamine and PCP-type drugs. They disconnect perception from the body and can injure the bladder, brain, or heart.

classes.name: Cannabinoid
classes.description: THC, related plant cannabinoids, and synthetic cannabinoids. The synthetic group is far more physically dangerous.

classes.name: Antidepressant
classes.description: Medicines for depression and anxiety. MAOIs in this class are dangerous with stimulants, SSRIs, and many other drugs.

classes.name: Antipsychotic
classes.description: Medicines for psychosis and some mood disorders. They add sedation and, for several, heart-rhythm and metabolic risk.

classes.name: Anaesthetic
classes.description: Hospital anaesthetics and local anaesthetics. Outside a monitored setting they cause stopped breathing, heart rhythm collapse, or both.

classes.name: Inhalant
classes.description: Gases, volatile solvents, and nitrites. Solvents can cause sudden heart death. Nitrites are a different and still serious risk.

classes.name: Plant / Fungi
classes.description: Plants and fungi that contain psychoactive or toxic compounds. Strength varies by specimen. Some are outright poisons.

classes.name: Research chemical
classes.description: Unregulated substances sold under chemical names. The tablet or powder is often a different drug from the label, and toxicity data are thin.

classes.name: Prescription
classes.description: Medicines that matter because they change the risk of other substances: bleeding, serotonin, sedation, heart rhythm, or withdrawal.

classes.name: OTC
classes.description: Medicines sold without a prescription that still cause overdose, liver injury, sedation, or dangerous mixes.

classes.name: Withdrawn
classes.description: Medicines taken off major markets because of harm, plus toxic contaminants people did not mean to take.

classes.name: Historical
classes.description: Preparations and poisons from older medicine. The chemistry is still toxic when someone recreates it.

classes.name: Other
classes.description: Substances that do not sit cleanly in one class and still belong in the index because people meet them.

timeline.title: Morphine isolated
timeline.description: Morphine was isolated from opium, the start of modern opioid pharmacy and of a dependence problem that outlasted the century.

timeline.title: Cocaine isolated
timeline.description: Cocaine was isolated from coca leaf. Later medical enthusiasm missed the heart and dependence harms.

timeline.title: Diacetylmorphine made
timeline.description: Diacetylmorphine, later sold as heroin, was first made in a laboratory. This archive does not describe that chemistry.

timeline.title: Heroin marketed
timeline.description: Heroin was sold as a medicine and a cough remedy. Dependence followed at population scale.

timeline.title: MDMA first made
timeline.description: MDMA was first synthesised. Widespread nonmedical use came much later. This archive does not describe the synthesis.

timeline.title: Harrison Act
timeline.description: The United States restricted opioids and cocaine through the Harrison Narcotics Tax Act. Control has never been uniform worldwide.

timeline.title: Alcohol prohibition
timeline.description: National alcohol prohibition in the United States showed both the harm of the drug and the harm of an unregulated supply.

timeline.title: LSD synthesised
timeline.description: LSD was first made in a pharmaceutical laboratory. The archive does not describe that synthesis.

timeline.title: LSD exposure described
timeline.description: An accidental exposure made LSD's potency obvious. Potency is why blotter sold as LSD is sometimes a more toxic substitute.

timeline.title: Chlorpromazine introduced
timeline.description: Chlorpromazine opened the era of antipsychotic medicines, with sedation and movement harms of its own.

timeline.title: Chlordiazepoxide released
timeline.description: The first benzodiazepine reached the market and largely replaced barbiturates, then produced its own dependence crisis.

timeline.title: Single Convention
timeline.description: The UN Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs became the template for national drug control.

timeline.title: Thalidomide withdrawn
timeline.description: Thalidomide was pulled after severe birth defects. Withdrawn does not mean gone from unregulated markets.

timeline.title: US smoking report
timeline.description: The US Surgeon General's report tied cigarettes to cancer and heart disease in public health terms.

timeline.title: US Controlled Substances Act
timeline.description: The United States built its modern scheduling system. Schedules are legal categories, not a measure of safety.

timeline.title: UN Psychotropic Convention
timeline.description: International control expanded to many stimulants, depressants, and psychedelics.

timeline.title: MPTP parkinsonism
timeline.description: Contaminated synthetic opioid material caused sudden, permanent parkinsonism. The toxin was MPTP. This archive does not describe how it forms.

timeline.title: MDMA emergency scheduling
timeline.description: The United States emergency-scheduled MDMA. Nonmedical use and clinical research then followed different tracks.

timeline.title: Crack and the unregulated supply
timeline.description: Smoked cocaine became a public-health crisis. The route changes speed, not the fact that cocaine strains the heart.

timeline.title: California medical cannabis
timeline.description: The first US state medical-cannabis law passed. Laws still differ sharply by country and state.

timeline.title: Modern psilocybin research
timeline.description: Clinical research into psilocybin resumed under controlled conditions. Research settings are not a dose or a source.

timeline.title: Fentanyl in the illicit supply
timeline.description: Fentanyl and analogues became a dominant cause of opioid deaths in North America. Naloxone and drug checking are responses, not guarantees.

timeline.title: Carfentanil appears
timeline.description: Carfentanil, an opioid used for large animals, was identified in street opioids. Ordinary reagent tests do not measure it.

timeline.title: Esketamine approved
timeline.description: A nasal esketamine product was approved for treatment-resistant depression in the United States, inside a medical programme.

timeline.title: Nitazenes detected
timeline.description: Nitazene opioids began appearing in drug-checking data. They add another unknown-strength opioid to an already contaminated supply.

timeline.title: Xylazine spread
timeline.description: The veterinary sedative xylazine was found more often in opioid supplies. Naloxone does not reverse the xylazine sedation.

rules.note: Opioids and benzodiazepines both slow breathing. Together they are a common cause of fatal overdose. Naloxone reverses only the opioid part, and it can wear off first.
Opioids plus alcohol, GHB, barbiturates, or other sedatives multiply the chance that breathing stops.
Two opioids stack on the same receptors. The breathing risk is not an average of the two. Naloxone may need repeating.
Combining benzodiazepines deepens sedation and memory loss. Breathing risk rises again if any opioid or alcohol is also present.
Benzodiazepines with alcohol or other sedatives can stop breathing and cause choking during unconsciousness.
Two sedatives together, including alcohol with GHB, can cause coma and stopped breathing.
Two stimulants add strain on the heart, temperature, and blood pressure. Seizures and overheating become more likely.
A stimulant can hide sedation, then the sedative shows through suddenly. The heart is under strain the whole time.
A stimulant can mask how sedated an opioid has made someone. Breathing can fail as the stimulant wears off.
Stimulants with MAO inhibitors can cause a hypertensive crisis: severe headache, chest pain, and stroke.
MAO inhibitors with SSRIs, SNRIs, many antidepressants, or other serotonergic drugs can cause serotonin syndrome: rigidity, agitation, high temperature, and seizures.
Several opioids become much more dangerous with an MAOI. Tramadol with an MAOI is a particular serotonin and seizure risk and should be treated as deadly.
Tramadol with an MAOI can cause severe serotonin syndrome and seizures.
Tramadol plus an SSRI or SNRI raises the chance of serotonin syndrome and of seizures.
DXM with an MAOI can cause severe serotonin syndrome.
DXM plus an SSRI or SNRI can cause serotonin toxicity. Cough medicines are an easy way to take this mix without noticing.
Alcohol and cocaine form cocaethylene in the body. It lasts longer and adds strain on the heart.
Nitrites and medicines such as sildenafil both widen blood vessels. Together they can collapse blood pressure.
Dissociatives plus alcohol or other sedatives deepen unconsciousness and the chance of vomiting while unprotected.
Dissociatives plus benzodiazepines deepen sedation and the chance of choking.
Dissociatives plus opioids raise the chance of stopped breathing and of being unable to protect the airway.
Inhalants plus sedatives deepen unconsciousness. Volatile solvents can also trigger a fatal heart rhythm.
Volatile solvents sensitise the heart. A stimulant, fright, or sudden effort can trigger a fatal rhythm.
Cannabis can intensify impairment from alcohol or other sedatives. This is not a clearance to drive or to add an opioid.
Cannabis can add to opioid sedation. It does not remove the breathing risk of the opioid.
The mix can raise heart rate and anxiety. Synthetic cannabinoids are a separate and much sharper risk.
Classic psychedelics with lithium have been associated with seizures and a much more dangerous experience.
Psychedelics plus tramadol add seizure risk and serotonin risk.
SSRIs and SNRIs often blunt psychedelics and do not make them safe. Some combinations add serotonin risk.
Psychedelics plus MAOIs can cause serotonin syndrome and blood-pressure crisis. Ayahuasca already contains an MAOI.
NSAIDs plus warfarin raise the chance of serious bleeding.
NSAIDs can raise lithium levels and cause lithium toxicity: tremor, confusion, and vomiting.
Disulfiram with alcohol causes flushing, vomiting, and sometimes a dangerous heart and blood-pressure reaction.
Regular heavy alcohol use plus paracetamol raises the chance of liver injury. This file gives no safe amount of either.
Clozapine with benzodiazepines has been linked with collapse and dangerous sedation.
Xylazine deepens unconsciousness in opioid supplies. Naloxone does not reverse the xylazine. Breathing support still matters.
Levamisole in cocaine has been linked with immune collapse, skin injury, and vasculitis.
Antipsychotics add sedation. With an opioid, the person can become deeply unconscious and stop protecting their airway.
Antipsychotics plus alcohol or other sedatives deepen unconsciousness and low blood pressure.
Two drugs that prolong the QT interval raise the chance of a dangerous heart rhythm.
